## In Layman's Terms

Motion capture connects pictures or wearable-sensor readings to an estimate of how a golfer moves. Each connection matters: where the cameras are, when they record, how skin moves over bone, and what the software means by a “rotation.” A convincing animation alone cannot tell us how much energy moved through a joint or which muscles caused the motion.

**Define the question first.** Clubface orientation just before impact, pelvis turn during the downswing, and shoulder-joint loading are different measurements. A system can answer one well and struggle with another. Its advertised accuracy needs to refer to the quantity you actually want.

**Skin is not bone.** A marker follows the skin it is attached to. Like tracking a person by watching their coat, this can reveal the overall movement while misrepresenting a local turn. Cameras can locate the marker very precisely without locating the underlying bone equally well.

**One swing, several descriptions.** Different rotation conventions can give different angle values for the same orientation. Screw axes offer another useful description, but still require a reference frame and sufficiently informative measurements. Changing the mathematics does not repair missing information.

**Key takeaway:** follow the chain from observation to inference to conclusion. A change in a graph becomes persuasive when its definition is clear, it exceeds the relevant uncertainty, and competing explanations have been tested.
:::


## Why This Article Exists

We want to understand how a golfer coordinates the body and club to deliver a particular impact: how earlier effort establishes motion and stored energy, how constraints redirect that motion, and what later actions can still change. Motion capture supplies indispensable evidence about that process. It measures neither muscle force nor the causal contribution of a movement directly.

The chain is **sensor observation → reconstruction → anatomical model → kinematic quantity → mechanical interpretation**. Timing and uncertainty enter every stage. A smooth trajectory can result from a useful estimator, excessive filtering, or an overly restrictive model. A segment-speed peak can be repeatable without identifying an energy-transfer mechanism. Conversely, uncertainty does not make measurement futile: it tells us which distinctions the experiment can support.

Begin with the *measurand*: the quantity intended to be measured. “Shoulder rotation” is incomplete. Is it humerus relative to scapula, scapula relative to thorax, or a line through the acromia relative to the room? At what event, with what axes and convention? This article develops the geometry and error structure needed to make those questions answerable.

## Part I: Reconstruction and Its Conditioning {#part-i-reconstruction-the-well-posed-part}

### From Image to Ray

A calibrated pinhole camera maps a homogeneous world point $\tilde X$ to an undistorted image coordinate $\tilde x$ through $\tilde x\sim P\tilde X$, where $P=K[R\mid t]$. Here $K$ contains intrinsics, and $R,t$ map world coordinates into camera coordinates. Real observations also require a lens-distortion model. An optical marker may be localized to a fraction of a pixel; that is image localization precision, not yet a three-dimensional accuracy claim. See the [OpenCV calibration and reconstruction model](https://docs.opencv.org/4.13.0/d9/d0c/group__calib3d.html).

For corresponding observations of the **same point at the same time**, each calibrated image defines a viewing ray. A linear triangulation initialization stacks constraints

$$
\tilde x_i\times(P_i\tilde X)=0.
$$

Noise generally prevents exact ray intersection. A fit may then minimize image reprojection error; a bundle adjustment can jointly refine camera and point parameters. Neither method creates missing geometric information. Small intersection angles, uncertain distortion, occlusion, mistaken marker identities and unsynchronized cameras can make the result poor even when an optimizer returns a smooth answer. With coincident camera centres, additional orientations alone do not supply a stereo baseline for an isolated point.

A rectified two-camera example makes the sensitivity visible. With focal length $f$ in pixels, baseline $B$ in metres and disparity $d$ in pixels, depth is $Z=fB/d$. Holding calibrated $f,B$ fixed, a small disparity standard uncertainty $\sigma_d$ gives

$$
\sigma_Z\approx\frac{Z^2}{fB}\sigma_d.
$$

**Manufactured example:** $f=1000$ pixels, $Z=5$ m, $B=1$ m and $\sigma_d=0.2$ pixels give approximately **5 mm** depth uncertainty. Reducing the baseline to $0.2$ m raises it to **25 mm**. These are local sensitivities under stated assumptions, not specifications for a product. Calibration uncertainty adds further terms. Wider baselines can improve depth conditioning but also make shared visibility and correspondence harder.

### What That Number Does and Does Not Mean

A reprojection residual is commonly expressed in pixels; a three-dimensional wand-length error or reconstruction residual may be expressed in millimetres. They measure different things. Small residuals show internal consistency with a fitted model. They do not, by themselves, establish external accuracy, correct scale, anatomical validity, or performance at the edge of the volume during a fast swing.

Validate against a reference with characterized uncertainty, using the relevant locations, speeds, marker sizes, lighting and occlusions. Report bias, dispersion and failure frequency separately. Test withheld calibration poses or independent distances rather than only the observations used to fit the model. A system can have repeatable error; a more flexible fit can reduce residuals while weakening generalization.

## Part II: Soft Tissue Artefact and Anatomical Inference {#part-ii-soft-tissue-artefact-the-dominant-error}

A skin marker is not rigidly attached to bone. Its relative displacement can depend on posture, acceleration, muscle contraction, location, attachment and the participant. Soft tissue artefact (STA) includes repeatable movement-dependent components and variable components. It is often consequential, but its dominance must be established for the particular outcome rather than assumed for every experiment.

A concrete example is [Fiorentino et al. (2017)](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.gaitpost.2017.03.033): eleven asymptomatic young adults performed walking, hip abduction and hip rotation while skin markers and dual fluoroscopy were recorded. Mean STA across marker/activity combinations ranged from **3 to 54 mm**. Skin-marker estimates were, on average, **5.8° more internally rotated**; the largest internal–external rotation range difference was **21.8°** during the hip-rotation task. These are hip results for those protocols, not an error allowance for a golfer's scapula or clubface.

Filtering can attenuate high-frequency components; it cannot reliably separate artefact from bone motion when their temporal and spatial patterns overlap. Repetition reduces independent random components, not a persistent bias. A rigid cluster helps estimate its own pose, but the whole cluster can move relative to bone. Three-dimensional reconstruction of an undeformed cluster does not establish a correct anatomical pose.

Anatomical calibration relates the cluster to landmarks or functional joint motion. Errors in palpation, joint-centre estimation and the assumed joint model are additional mechanisms. Joint constraints and multibody fitting can reject implausible configurations, but a wrong constraint can redistribute error into other joints. In the hip study above, model constraints did not consistently reduce angle errors. Inspect residual patterns and sensitivity to plausible anatomy instead of judging a model only by how smooth its output looks.

The downstream issue is mechanical as well as geometric. A force's moment about a specified point is $M=r\times F$. If its lever arm has error $\delta r$ while $F$ is held fixed, then $\delta M=\delta r\times F$. A manufactured **10 mm** perpendicular lever-arm error under **1000 N** produces a **10 N·m** moment error. The same location error parallel to the force produces zero moment error. Direction and the intended output determine importance; a millimetre value alone does not.

Direct bone imaging and invasive bone-fixed markers avoid the skin-to-bone tracking step, with different practical and ethical constraints. They still require calibration, registration and a declared anatomical coordinate system.

## Part III: The Rotation Problem

### Euler Angles and Sequence Dependence

Let $R_P$ and $R_T$ map pelvis and thorax coordinates into a common laboratory frame. The thorax orientation expressed in pelvis coordinates is $R_{PT}=R_P^T R_T$. This is a relative **orientation**. Its three reported Euler/Cardan coordinates depend on an ordered sequence, axis conventions, signs and reference posture. Acromial-line rotation is a different construction again; it includes shoulder-girdle motion and need not equal anatomical thorax rotation.

Finite rotations generally do not commute, so adding angle triples does not compose orientations. However, this does **not** make every coordinate average meaningless. Within a declared nonsingular chart, an unwrapped angle mean can summarize that coordinate. Near wrap boundaries or gimbal lock it may be misleading. An orientation mean on $SO(3)$ instead requires a distance/objective and weights; uniqueness is not guaranteed globally. See the [rotation reference](rotation-representations-reference.html) for conventions and stable boundary cases.

Gimbal lock makes some angle decompositions nonunique or ill-conditioned while the physical orientation remains defined. Another representation can avoid that chart singularity. It does not recover an anatomical axis or an unobserved degree of freedom. Standardized joint coordinate systems improve comparability when their anatomical definitions and calibration are also followed; merely stating a rotation sequence is insufficient.

### The Helical Axis Alternative

For a rigid body's velocity field in one declared observer frame, choose a reference point $O$. Let $v_O$ be the body's velocity field evaluated at that point and let $r$ be displacement from it. All components below use the same orthonormal basis, with angular velocity in radians per second:

$$
v(r)=v_O+\omega\times r.
$$

For $\|\omega\|>0$, the closest point of the instantaneous screw axis to $O$ and the pitch are

$$
r_0=\frac{\omega\times v_O}{\|\omega\|^2},
\qquad h=\frac{\omega\cdot v_O}{\|\omega\|^2}.
$$

The axis is the line $r_0+\lambda\hat\omega$, with $\hat\omega=\omega/\|\omega\|$. Substitution gives $v(r_0)=h\omega$: points on the axis move along it. Pitch has units of length per radian, conventionally written metres in dimensional analysis. Rotation speed and pitch are separate quantities. If $\omega=0$ and $v_O\ne0$, the motion is pure translation with no finite unique axis; if both vanish, no axis is selected at all.

A finite relative displacement likewise has a screw description when its rotational part is nonidentity. Its finite angle and axial translation concern the two endpoint poses, not the entire intervening path. An interval estimate approaches instantaneous motion only under suitable smoothness and estimation conditions. Rotation-branch choices and degenerate cases must be specified.

Screw geometry removes the Euler **sequence** choice. It retains the choice of moving body, reference body, interval and statistic. Under a rigid change of coordinates describing the same velocity field, its line transforms geometrically and pitch is unchanged. A different moving observer changes the relative velocity field and can change pitch. Thus “frame independent” needs qualification; it does not mean “relative to anything.”

**Manufactured example:** $\omega=(0,0,2)$ rad/s and $v_O=(1,0,0.2)$ m/s give $r_0=(0,0.5,0)$ m and $h=0.1$ m/rad. An observer translating at $0.2$ m/s along the same $z$ direction measures zero axial translation and zero pitch. Neither description is erroneous. The physical question determines which relative motion matters.

#### The Caveat That Matters More Than the Advocacy

Axis estimation divides by rotational magnitude and therefore becomes sensitive when that magnitude is small compared with its uncertainty. Suppose a true angular velocity $(0,0,\Omega)$ is contaminated by a perpendicular $0.01$ rad/s error. The direction error is $\arctan(0.01/\Omega)$: approximately **0.573°** at $\Omega=1$ rad/s and **45°** at $\Omega=0.01$ rad/s. The algebra remains valid while the estimated direction becomes uninformative.

For finite rotations, orientation error relative to a small net rotation has a similar conditioning problem. Marker separation and noncollinearity determine how well rotation can be estimated; a longer time interval can improve rotational separation but changes temporal resolution and may average changing motion. Reversals can also leave a small net rotation over a long interval. Gate estimates by uncertainty relative to signal, report excluded intervals, and test sensitivity to filtering and window length. A fixed speed threshold is a protocol choice, not a universal validity boundary.

At the top of a golf backswing, a selected club-path component may reverse while other components of three-dimensional motion remain nonzero. Do not infer that the entire angular-velocity vector vanishes. A club-mounted cluster avoids skin artefact, but small or nearly collinear clusters, occlusion, attachment motion and shaft deformation can still compromise it. Treat grip and head as distinct bodies when a rigid whole-club approximation is inadequate.

### How Large Is the Convention Effect?

[Karduna et al. (2000)](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/10854878/) reported differences up to **50° for some scapular angles** when changing the Euler sequence. This demonstrates dependence of the reported coordinates, not a 50° camera error. The [Bourgain et al. review (2022)](https://doi.org/10.3390/sports10060091) distinguishes torso–pelvis from shoulder–pelvis definitions of X-factor, with reported values around 30° and 60° across the relevant studies. Those values are not a controlled demonstration that changing one setting doubles every golfer's same physical measurement.

Before comparing studies, establish whether their quantities are transformable descriptions of the same motion or different anatomical constructs. Converting angle coordinates can reconcile the former when the full orientation and conventions are available. It cannot turn a shoulder-girdle line into a measured thoracic bone frame.

## Part IIIb: An Error Budget for a Defined Outcome {#part-iiib-the-error-budget-ordered}

A table of camera millimetres, palpation millimetres, hip-angle degrees and shoulder convention differences is **not a ranked uncertainty budget**. It mixes units, tasks and estimands. Instead, define an output $y=g(z)$ from the relevant measurements and calibration/model inputs $z$. For a smooth local approximation, with covariance $\Sigma_z$ and Jacobian $J$, propagated covariance is

$$
\Sigma_y\approx J\Sigma_zJ^T.
$$

This expresses the [GUM approach to measurement uncertainty](https://www.bipm.org/en/committees/jc/jcgm/wg/jcgm-wg1-gum). It needs a suitable model, input uncertainties and correlations. Uncorrected bias, discrete mislabelling, model discrepancy, censoring and singularities are not automatically covered by a small Gaussian covariance. Use scenario analysis or distribution propagation when linearization is inadequate, and preserve the dependence between inputs.

| Stage | Question to Ask | Check at the Intended Output |
|---|---|---|
| Images and calibration | Are scale, geometry, identity and visibility adequate? | Independent dynamic reconstruction tests across the volume |
| Timing | Are samples synchronized, sufficiently frequent and sharply exposed? | Perturb timestamps and processing windows; inspect event uncertainty |
| Anatomy | How do landmarks, skin and model constraints affect bone pose? | Repeat setup; vary plausible anatomy; compare an appropriate reference |
| Representation | Are body, frame, sequence and event definitions the same? | Reconcile definitions before comparing values |
| Interpretation | Does the output distinguish the proposed mechanisms? | Propagate to the actual outcome and test competing explanations |

Relative quantities need particular care. For scalar turn coordinates $\theta_T,\theta_P$ under a common convention,

$$
\operatorname{var}(\theta_T-\theta_P)
=\sigma_T^2+\sigma_P^2-2\operatorname{cov}(\theta_T,\theta_P).
$$

With **2°** standard uncertainty in each coordinate, independent errors give **2.83°** in their difference. Correlation $0.75$ reduces it to **1.41°**; correlation $-0.75$ raises it to **3.74°**. These are manufactured examples. Differencing does not invariably amplify error. Indeed, an identical laboratory-frame rotation error $S$ cancels exactly in the full relative orientation: $(SR_P)^T(SR_T)=R_P^TR_T$. Independent anatomical calibration errors generally do not cancel. [The VIM's compatibility definition](https://jcgm.bipm.org/vim/en/2.47.html) explicitly retains correlation.

Differentiation changes the problem again. For independent position errors with standard deviation $\sigma_x$, the central second difference has acceleration standard deviation $\sqrt{6}\sigma_x/\Delta t^2$. At **1 mm** and **10 ms**, that is **24.5 m/s²** before filtering. It is not a forecast for a smoothed motion-capture pipeline: smoothing changes temporal correlation, bandwidth and bias. It explains why accurate-looking positions do not guarantee accurate inverse-dynamics loads, and why increasing sample rate without redesigning the estimator need not reduce derivative noise.

::: {.callout-note}
## The Connection to the Rest of This Section

A motion twist and a load wrench are dual through power, not interchangeable measurements. At a shared point and in a shared observer frame, $P=F\cdot v_O+M_O\cdot\omega$. Both the velocity axis and a wrench's central axis involve divisions that become ill-conditioned as the relevant rotational or force magnitude vanishes. This geometry helps organize the calculation; forces, moments and their uncertainty still need independent evidence. See [force measurement](technology-force-measurement.html) and [launch-monitor technology](technology-launch-monitors.html).
:::

## Part IV: The System Families and What Each Trades Away

### Optical Marker-Based

Cameras identify reflective or active markers and reconstruct their motion. Strengths include explicit geometric observations and the ability to instrument body segments and equipment. Limitations include preparation, occlusion, misidentification, reflective clutter, calibration and skin artefact. Uniquely coded active markers can reduce identity ambiguity, but visibility, decoding and attachment remain relevant; active systems need not all use the same wiring architecture.

The useful specification separates marker reconstruction from segment pose, anatomical joint quantities and club delivery. A static marker-position result is insufficient evidence for a head-orientation result at impact. Cluster geometry and rigid-body fit residuals help identify failures, but an apparently rigid cluster can still be displaced relative to the intended body.

### Markerless

Video pipelines may detect two-dimensional keypoints and triangulate them, infer depth from a single image using priors, fit a body mesh, or combine these approaches over time. The output combines image information with learned and mechanical assumptions. More cameras can improve visibility and depth information; more useful views, synchronization and calibration matter as much as the count.

[OpenCap's 2023 validation](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pcbi.1011462) illustrates how to bound a result: ten adults performed walking, squats, sit-to-stand and drop jumps. Its two-camera HRNet setup had **4.5° mean absolute error**, averaged over 18 rotational degrees of freedom and activities, against a marker-based modelling pipeline. The reported range across those conditions/coordinates was 1.7–10.3°. The paper also describes alignment, model assumptions and camera/pose-estimator sensitivity tests. This supports those tested uses; it does not establish 4.5° accuracy for a shoulder's axial rotation in a full-speed golf swing or directly validate inferred muscle force.

Agreement with skin-marker capture is not identical to bone-pose accuracy. Both systems have errors, potentially correlated through shared models or calibration. Disagreement cannot all be assigned to the markerless system, nor does similar aggregate error prove a common irreducible noise floor.

#### Why Axial Rotation Can Be Weakly Observed {#why-axial-rotation-fails-three-independent-causes}

**Landmark geometry:** two known endpoints define a segment line but leave rotation about that line undetermined. In ideal three-dimensional rigid-body tracking, three corresponding noncollinear points determine pose. For a camera pipeline, those points must first be localized and reconstructed well. Additional labelled surface features, temporal information and joint constraints may help, but a plausible prior-driven roll is not the same as directly observed roll.

**Appearance:** an approximately symmetric surface can change little under axial rotation. Clothing, occlusion and small projected displacements may weaken the signal further. This is conditional on the surface, viewpoint and task; it is not a theorem that every transverse-plane quantity is always less accurate than every sagittal-plane quantity.

**Model anatomy:** a model optimized for plausible skin deformation need not have anatomically calibrated joint centres or distributed forearm motion. The [SKEL research](https://download.is.tue.mpg.de/skel/main_paper.pdf) explicitly addresses the mapping from surface shape to a biomechanical skeleton. Model family names alone do not determine what a particular pipeline measures: inspect its degrees of freedom, observations, constraints and validation. A visually convincing animation is insufficient evidence of anatomical fidelity.

#### Labels, Models and Images All Matter {#the-error-is-in-the-labels-not-the-network}

Training annotations can introduce systematic landmark bias; a network may learn an inconsistent definition accurately. This is one mechanism among image noise, domain shift, occlusion, geometry and modelling error. Comparing different systems with one, two and ten cameras does not isolate the effect of camera count, because algorithms, training, anatomy and calibration also change.

To test a bottleneck, vary it while holding the relevant alternatives fixed. Assess held-out people and capture conditions; report failures and excluded swings. A benchmark that aligns away position, rotation or scale before scoring answers a different question from absolute anatomical accuracy. Extra cameras cannot resolve a genuinely unobserved anatomical distinction by themselves, but they can substantially improve an otherwise poorly conditioned measurement.

#### Two Framings Worth Keeping Straight

**Offset versus waveform:** an offset correction may improve a comparison if the offset is stable and independently calibrated. It can conceal the quantity of interest if estimated anew from every test trial. Fit calibration on separate data and evaluate whether it transfers. Good between-session repeatability can help detect change, but does not guarantee sensitivity to a small real change or validity of comparisons with population norms.

**Skin versus skeleton:** removing attached markers removes their placement step; it does not remove the need to infer bone motion from external appearance. Conversely, it need not inherit the same error magnitude or covariance as a marker set. Calibration and better anatomical modelling can help. The direction and amount of improvement require evidence for the specific pipeline and task.

### Inertial

An IMU's gyroscope measures angular velocity with bias and noise; its accelerometer measures **specific force**, approximately $a-g$ expressed in sensor coordinates, rather than position or gravity alone. A magnetometer, when present, measures local magnetic field. Sensor fusion estimates orientation; under strong movement acceleration, accelerometer readings cannot simply be treated as a gravity direction.

Integrating biased angular velocity causes orientation error; integrating acceleration requires orientation, gravity compensation, initial conditions and bias estimation. Accelerometer–gyroscope integration alone does not generally bound absolute position or heading error. Magnetic, visual, contact or linked-body constraints can improve observability under their own assumptions. Magnetic disturbances, sensor saturation, soft-tissue attachment, timing and sensor-to-anatomy alignment remain material. Freedom from camera line-of-sight is useful; it is not freedom from every operating limit.

The golf validation discussed below supports defined torso/pelvis summary measures in one protocol. It should not be transferred to clubhead position, every anatomical joint or another manufacturer's hardware without additional evidence.

### Videoradiography as a Reference {#videoradiography-the-benchmark}

Biplanar radiography observes bone through two views and can register bone models to those images. It bypasses skin-marker artefact and can characterize errors in practical methods, as in the hip study above. Calibration, imaging quality, model registration and reference-frame definitions still matter. Accuracy is protocol-specific. Radiation, capture volume, access and equipment constraints limit use; it is neither a universal whole-swing solution nor an infallible reference.

### Emerging Modalities

Depth cameras, LiDAR and radar introduce different depth, reflectance, spatial-resolution and interference trade-offs. Event cameras report brightness changes asynchronously rather than integrating conventional frames. That can reduce conventional exposure-blur limitations, but temporal response, thresholds, event noise, bandwidth and reconstruction still constrain motion estimates. The [event-vision literature](https://arxiv.org/abs/1904.08405) describes the sensing distinction; it does not itself validate anatomical golf measurements. A sensor demonstration and a validated biomechanics pipeline are different achievements.

::: {.callout-note}
## Choosing by Error Structure, Not by Specification Sheet

Choose a system by testing whether its output uncertainty is small enough for the decision you need. A repeated within-golfer pelvis-turn comparison, a clubface reconstruction near contact, and a joint-load estimate have different requirements. Ask what was observed, what was inferred, which failures were excluded, and whether the validation reproduces your task and setup.
:::

## Part V: Golf-Specific Practice

### The Temporal Problem, Quantified

At a stipulated constant clubhead speed of **45 m/s**, travel between successive frames is $v/f_s$:

| Capture Rate | Frame Period | Travel Between Frames |
|---|---|---|
| 200 Hz | 5 ms | 22.5 cm |
| 300 Hz | 3.33 ms | 15 cm |
| 360 Hz | 2.78 ms | 12.5 cm |
| 500 Hz | 2 ms | 9 cm |
| 1000 Hz | 1 ms | 4.5 cm |

This displacement affects association, gap filling and event timing. **Exposure blur depends on exposure duration**, not frame period: at 45 m/s, a 50 microsecond exposure spans **2.25 mm** of physical travel. Its image blur depends on projected velocity and magnification. A short exposure at 300 Hz can freeze a marker while leaving 15 cm between observations; it does not fill that temporal gap. Rolling-shutter row timing can distort a moving object even when each row has a short exposure.

Synchronization is separate again. A **1 ms** offset between cameras corresponds to **45 mm** of head travel in this example. Triangulating their observations as simultaneous can create a geometric inconsistency. At 300 Hz, rounding an event to the nearest sample has a best-case discretization bound of **±1.67 ms**, before event-definition and measurement uncertainty. Interpolation can improve an estimate when justified by a trajectory model; it does not reveal arbitrary subframe dynamics.

Sampling must match signal bandwidth, not merely peak speed. Even ideal instantaneous samples of a 220 Hz sinusoid at 300 Hz are indistinguishable from a signed 80 Hz alias. Short exposure does not solve aliasing. Filtering and fitted trajectories should be tested against the fastest feature needed, including their effect on relative peak times. Offline zero-phase filtering avoids a simple phase lag but can still alter peaks, boundaries and transient shapes; it is not a causal real-time estimator.

::: {.callout-warning}
## Body Motion and Contact Dynamics {#a-figure-that-does-not-survive-checking}

Pelvis or thorax peak speeds do not bound distal-segment angular speed. Neither a sensor's full-scale range nor linear clubhead speed divided by an arbitrary lever arm is a measured joint angular velocity. Specify segment, relative frame and scalar before comparing numbers. Likewise, submillisecond club–ball contact is compatible with much slower body-motion sampling; such a record cannot resolve the contact force waveform. See [launch-monitor technology](technology-launch-monitors.html) for the distinction between contact duration, sampling and inferred impact quantities. An unsuccessful citation search is not evidence that a physical timescale is impossible.
:::

### Commercial Golf Systems

The following descriptions were checked against the linked sources on **9 September 2026**. They distinguish vendor documentation from independent experiments; they are not a ranking or a guarantee about all product versions.

**GEARS:** the [vendor's golf page](https://www.gearssports.com/golf-swing-biomechanics/) describes eight 1.7-megapixel cameras at 360 frames/s, tracking grip and head, and measurements as fine as 0.2 mm. The page does not make that number an independently established dynamic anatomical-angle error bound. Ask for the installed camera configuration, calibration procedure, rigid-body definitions and validation of the intended club/body output.

**K-MOTION/K-VEST:** the [manufacturer's FAQ](https://www.k-motion.com/faqs/how-is-the-k-vest-different-from-other-3d-products-on-the-market/) describes a four-sensor K-VEST configuration. Sensor count is product/configuration dependent. It is incorrect to identify the following custom research system as a validation of that commercial product.

**A research IMU comparison:** [Kim et al. (2023)](https://doi.org/10.3390/s23208433) studied 36 golfers using **two custom IMUs at 100 Hz**, placed at T1 and L4, with a defined optical comparison and processing protocol. Reported ICCs ranged from 0.91 to 1.00; these are not simply Pearson $r$. Table 3 gives upper-torso rotation mean difference 1.05° with limits of agreement **−11.16° to 13.26°**; X-factor mean difference −1.39° with limits **−21.35° to 18.56°**. Pelvic angular velocity has different units, degrees/s. Small average bias therefore does not mean every individual measurement is within one or two degrees. Assess agreement, exclusions and repeated-measures structure for the intended use, rather than correlation alone.

**Sportsbox AI:** its [vendor-authored accuracy report](https://help.sportsbox.ai/sportsbox-ai-accuracy) compares one swing each from 30 golfers with AMM3D, an electromagnetic system. It reports mean absolute angular differences of **2.2°, 2.5° and 2.0°** at address, top and impact for selected torso/pelvis measures. Mean linear differences were **0.6 in** at top and **0.2 in** at impact; averaging these gives the headline 0.4 in. These are neither per-swing maximum errors nor full-trajectory joint-angle bounds. The report describes good lighting, camera positioning and a fast shutter. That evidence should be credited with its provenance and scope; it does not establish accuracy for every app output or uncontrolled camera placement.

### The Kinematic Sequence, and Why It Is Less Settled Than It Appears

A sequence of segment-speed peaks requires choices: global or relative angular velocity, vector norm or component, filtering, event boundaries and treatment of multiple peaks. A component about a body axis, a component about a laboratory axis and the derivative of a Cardan angle are generally different scalars. Even perfect orientation data do not make them interchangeable.

[Marsan et al. (2019)](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31741482/) compared seven angular-velocity definitions in thirteen golfers. Identified sequences depended strongly on the chosen component; no method was established as a reference. This is a reason to declare and test a definition, not to abandon temporal coordination as a question. For example, a vector can have an early peak in its $x$ component and a larger later peak in its $y$ component; its norm can then peak after a second segment whose $x$ peak occurs in between. Different orderings can describe the same underlying vector trajectories.

The screw axis does not supply a unique replacement scalar or peak event. Its direction, position, pitch and rotation magnitude answer different questions. Norms remove dependence on a rotated orthonormal basis for the same vector, but changing the reference body changes the motion being compared. Peak-time confidence intervals and sensitivity to reasonable processing choices belong alongside an ordering, especially when peaks are close or flat.

X-factor needs the same discipline. A thorax–pelvis orientation, a difference between projected line angles and a shoulder–pelvis measure are not interchangeable. Their covariance matters, as Part IIIb shows. A measured separation does not identify elastic energy: that requires tissue mechanics, loading history and a model of what actually deforms. Association with clubhead speed depends on population, task and confounders; absence of association in one restricted cohort does not prove that torso motion is mechanically irrelevant.

To connect coordination to transfer, estimate compatible motions and loads, then evaluate work and energy balances. At a grip interface, force times point velocity and moment times angular velocity both contribute. Joint net power is not a unique muscle-power decomposition. Ground force can change momentum without doing work at an ideal stationary no-slip contact. Earlier actions can establish velocity, activation and elastic state that influence later motion; a speed-peak diagram alone does not distinguish those mechanisms. [Inverse dynamics](inverse-dynamics.html) explains what additional assumptions enter the load calculation.

### Screw-Axis Analysis of the Golf Swing

Screw descriptions are valuable for organizing relative rigid motion. But **coordinate invariance is not conservation over time**, and stable pitch is not mechanical efficiency. For pure rotation about a stationary centre, pitch is zero at every speed. With fixed inertia, doubling angular velocity quadruples rotational kinetic energy while pitch remains zero. Thus pitch cannot by itself quantify transferred energy, dissipation or neural coordination.

[Kim (2025)](https://doi.org/10.3390/jfmk10030315) reanalyses two golfers. Its participant table labels the handicap-32, one-year player “proficient” and the handicap-8, fifteen-year player “novice,” an inconsistency that needs clarification before skill conclusions. The methods also discuss inertia-derived principal directions alongside kinematic screw axes. An inertia eigenvector is not generally the instantaneous axis of an observed velocity field. These constructs must be separated and the numerical derivation reproduced before treating a pitch contrast as a validated skill marker. The study is exploratory evidence, not proof that low pitch improves performance or reflects efficient energy transmission.

A stronger experiment would define club relative to thorax and club relative to ground separately; validate both rigid-body poses and timing; propagate uncertainty into axis/pitch estimates; and prespecify how low-rotation intervals are handled. Test repeatability and performance associations on held-out golfers and trials. Then compare interventions or validated forward-model predictions that separate alternative explanations. A correlation with vertical force alone does not identify grip work, torque transmission or a causal pathway.

That is the scientific opportunity: combine trustworthy motion estimates with force measurements and constrained dynamics, then ask which proposed mechanism predicts a distinguishable outcome. Better definitions make experiments comparable; better sensors and models make relevant distinctions measurable. Neither replaces the other.

## References and Further Reading

The inline references identify evidence at the claim it supports. Numerical examples labelled **manufactured** are calculations under stated assumptions, not measurements of golfers.

- **Measurement definitions and uncertainty:** [JCGM/BIPM guides](https://www.bipm.org/en/web/guest/publications/guides), including the GUM and supplements on propagation.
- **Anatomical conventions:** Wu and colleagues' ISB joint-coordinate recommendations, [Part I](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/11934426/) and [Part II](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15844264/). Report the specific convention and calibration rather than citing a standard generically.
- **Golf methods:** [Bourgain et al. (2022)](https://doi.org/10.3390/sports10060091), a systematic review of 92 articles; [Marsan et al. (2019)](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31741482/), a direct comparison of kinematic-sequence definitions.
- **Rigid motion:** [Modern Robotics](https://modernrobotics.northwestern.edu/chapters/chapter3/), Chapter 3, and the site's [rotation reference](rotation-representations-reference.html). Keep the angular-first/linear-first twist convention explicit.

::: {.callout-note}
## A Note on Sourcing

Empirical results retain their participants, tasks, quantities and reference methods. Vendor pages document their own claims; they do not substitute for independent validation. Earlier cross-study rankings, unsupported universal accuracy statements and assertions of absent literature have been withdrawn. The [technical review](https://github.com/D-sorganization/AffineDrift/blob/main/docs/development/technical-review/motion-capture-review.md) records the corrections and source-reading boundaries.
:::
